fabrics.title: How to wash leggings and technical activewear
fabrics.description: Stretch knits, bonded seams, elastic fibres and special performance finishes can respond differently to heat, friction, detergent and softeners.
fabrics.lead: Stretch knits, bonded seams, elastic fibres and special performance finishes can respond differently to heat, friction, detergent and softeners.

sections.heading: Read the sewn-in care label first.
body: Start with the care tag, not a universal “cold wash only” slogan. Turn inside out when helpful for surface abrasion, separate rough fasteners and check any product-specific detergent instructions.

sections.heading: The step that can change a garment.
body: Heat-sensitive elastic or bonded details can be a reason for low-temperature or no-tumble instructions. However, waterproof shells sometimes specifically benefit from controlled drying when the maker permits it.

sections.heading: What not to assume.
body: Do not apply one rule to all technical gear. A DWR-treated jacket can have different wash and dryer instructions from compression leggings; Patagonia documents garment-specific drying steps for shells.

sections.heading: Care symbols worth checking.
body: Only the garment's own symbols and manufacturer instructions can establish permitted temperatures, cycles or drying methods. This material article is not a personalized safety guarantee.

sections.heading: Material guidance is not a substitute for care labels.
body: There is no universal wash setting for every item made from activewear. Specific dyes, linings and finishes matter.

sections.heading: Read the sewn-in care label first.
body: Use the complete care sequence. A cotton-rich outer fabric does not override a restrictive instruction chosen because of a lining, elastic panel or dyed trim.

sections.heading: The step that can change a garment.
body: Respect the most specific printed drying method and temperature. If there are separate removable pieces with independent tags, care for each according to its own instructions.

sections.heading: What not to assume.
body: Avoid averaging the fibre composition into a guessed wash temperature. A label can be more restrictive than anything suggested by the material percentages.

fabrics.title: How to care for a cashmere sweater
fabrics.description: Cashmere is a fine animal fibre, and the garment construction can be more vulnerable than its soft feel suggests. A fibre label does not replace the finished g
fabrics.lead: Cashmere is a fine animal fibre, and the garment construction can be more vulnerable than its soft feel suggests. A fibre label does not replace the finished garment’s wash instruction.

sections.heading: Read the sewn-in care label first.
body: Inspect the actual wash tub and any printed note. When hand wash is allowed, handle gently and avoid rubbing, twisting or long unattended soaks. If the label prohibits washing, use the permitted professional method instead.

sections.heading: The step that can change a garment.
body: A washed cashmere knit is generally best supported flat and carefully reshaped; do not assume tumble drying is acceptable. Keep the item away from direct heater contact and check the care tag for shade-drying details.

sections.heading: What not to assume.
body: The common failure is washing a cashmere knit like an ordinary cotton tee, then lifting it by the shoulders while saturated. Mechanical action and wet stretching can both change the result.

sections.heading: Read the sewn-in care label first.
body: Use the temperature shown in the tub as an upper limit, not a goal. For dark or printed garments, separate by colour and turn inside out when the manufacturer advises it.

sections.heading: The step that can change a garment.
body: Do not assume every cotton garment may be tumble dried: cotton tees with elastane, graphics or special finishes may have a crossed dryer symbol.

sections.heading: What not to assume.
body: Bleaching, ironing and drying have separate symbols. A 60°C wash permission does not grant permission to use chlorine bleach or a hot iron.

fabrics.title: How to wash jeans and denim pieces
fabrics.description: Jeans are often cotton-rich, but dyes, stretch fibres, abrasions and special finishes change how a finished pair should be cleaned.
fabrics.lead: Jeans are often cotton-rich, but dyes, stretch fibres, abrasions and special finishes change how a finished pair should be cleaned.

sections.heading: Read the sewn-in care label first.
body: Read the jeans’ wash mark and any written inside-out or colour-transfer warning. New dark denim may release dye; sort with appropriate dark colours rather than a light or white load.

sections.heading: The step that can change a garment.
body: Follow the dryer mark, especially for stretch denim. Some jeans may permit low tumble drying; others specify line drying. A garment’s elastic recovery can be affected by overheating.

sections.heading: What not to assume.
body: Do not confuse visible fading from wear with proof that a bleach treatment is allowed. Only the triangle mark tells you whether bleaching is permitted.

fabrics.description: Linen fibres can withstand many common domestic processes, but a finished linen piece may have restrictive dyes, tailoring, lining or shrinkage-sensitive finis
fabrics.lead: Linen fibres can withstand many common domestic processes, but a finished linen piece may have restrictive dyes, tailoring, lining or shrinkage-sensitive finishes.

sections.heading: Read the sewn-in care label first.
body: Choose the printed tub temperature and cycle rather than a generic “hot wash linen” rule. New colours and mixed linen garments may need a gentler approach than a plain white household linen article.

sections.heading: The step that can change a garment.
body: Follow the square: some linen articles are line dried while others are suitable for tumble drying. Promptly removing the article from the washer can reduce creasing, but does not override the drying mark.

sections.heading: What not to assume.
body: A three-dot iron setting is only permitted if the iron mark actually shows it. Do not assume maximum ironing heat from the fibre name alone.

sections.heading: Read the sewn-in care label first.
body: Read the wash tub for the actual temperature and movement limit. Separate lint-shedding towels from smooth synthetics where practical, and respect any written detergent restrictions.

sections.heading: The step that can change a garment.
body: Use the drying mark rather than assuming synthetics can tolerate a hot dryer. Some pieces allow low heat while others need air drying to protect their construction.

sections.heading: What not to assume.
body: Do not set an iron to the cotton or linen setting because the garment appears thick. Check the iron dots and use a cloth when appropriate.

fabrics.title: How to wash silk clothing without guessing
fabrics.description: Silk garments may include delicate dyes, surface finishes, lining and trims. Two pure-silk pieces can have very different safe-care labels.
fabrics.lead: Silk garments may include delicate dyes, surface finishes, lining and trims. Two pure-silk pieces can have very different safe-care labels.

sections.heading: Read the sewn-in care label first.
body: Read both the wash permission and professional circle. If hand washing is explicitly allowed, use the specified temperature and gentle handling; if the tub is crossed, do not improvise with a cold rinse.

sections.heading: The step that can change a garment.
body: Avoid wringing silk. If the square includes a shade mark, use a shaded drying area; natural-dry directions may differ for dresses, scarves and structured garments.

sections.heading: What not to assume.
body: Do not infer bleach or ironing permission from fibre content. The triangle and iron marks are independent decisions, and many silk dyes or treatments can be affected by water or steam.

sections.heading: The step that can change a garment.
body: Respect a flat-dry or line-dry specification. Handle saturated garments carefully to prevent unwanted lengthening or distortion while the fibre is wet.

sections.heading: What not to assume.
body: The mistake is assuming an item is robust because it feels like cotton. Consult its finished garment care label and professional cleaning circle.

fabrics.title: How to wash wool without losing its shape
fabrics.description: Wool can felt or change shape when moisture, friction and heat combine. Some finished wool garments are machine-washable, while others are hand-wash or profess
fabrics.lead: Wool can felt or change shape when moisture, friction and heat combine. Some finished wool garments are machine-washable, while others are hand-wash or professional-care only.

sections.heading: Read the sewn-in care label first.
body: Check for a wool- or very-mild-cycle label, not merely the word “wool” on the composition tag. Washable wool can often use a dedicated wool program when the label allows it; tailored, lined or embellished pieces may need a different process.

sections.heading: The step that can change a garment.
body: For a wet sweater, support its full weight and reshape it on a pale, lint-free towel. Woolmark recommends flat drying knitwear unless the item specifically permits tumble drying; some approved wool items do permit a suitable low-heat dryer.

sections.heading: What not to assume.
body: Avoid treating all wool as dry-clean-only or all wool as machine-washable. Those are both unsafe shortcuts. Strong agitation and hanging a heavy wet knit can cause problems even when the water temperature is low.

guides.title: Bleach symbols explained: triangle, lines and cross
guides.description: An empty triangle, a triangle with two lines, and a crossed triangle give three different permissions. The small difference determines whether chlorine bleach,
guides.lead: An empty triangle, a triangle with two lines, and a crossed triangle give three different permissions. The small difference determines whether chlorine bleach, oxygen bleach or no bleach is permitted.

sections.heading: Empty triangle: bleach when appropriate
body: Both chlorine and oxygen bleaching are permitted by the symbol, but the product still must be used correctly. “Allowed” does not mean “required.”

sections.heading: Two diagonal lines: non-chlorine only
body: Choose an oxygen/non-chlorine product when bleaching is needed. Do not confuse a detergent’s marketing label with its actual ingredients.

sections.heading: Crossed triangle: none
body: Avoid all bleaching agents, including oxygen bleach and bleach-containing detergent additives.

sections.heading: Other symbols still apply
body: A bleach-permitted item can still have a restrictive washing temperature or drying method. Read the complete care label.

body: Care advice here summarizes published sources. We have not performed garment-specific laboratory tests. A damaged item may need professional assessment.

guides.title: My black clothes faded: can the colour come back?
guides.description: Colour loss may come from dye transfer, surface abrasion, detergent chemistry or light. If dye has actually left the fabric, an ordinary wash usually cannot re
guides.lead: Colour loss may come from dye transfer, surface abrasion, detergent chemistry or light. If dye has actually left the fabric, an ordinary wash usually cannot restore the original colour.

sections.heading: Check whether it is residue or dye loss
body: A powdery film may be detergent or lint; uneven pale patches may indicate chemical damage or abrasion. Do not add bleach to “brighten” dark clothing.

sections.heading: Avoid further colour damage
body: Sort darks from lights, follow the care-label temperature and bleach triangle, and avoid direct sun if the drying symbol specifies shade.

sections.heading: Be careful with dyeing
body: Home recolouring can stain stitching, elastics or trims differently, and may not be suitable for all fibre blends. Follow dye product and garment instructions before attempting it.

sections.heading: Prevent future fading
body: Read the laundry and drying marks as one set. The bleach triangle and corner-shade slash often explain decisions that temperature alone cannot.

body: Care advice here summarizes published sources. We have not performed garment-specific laboratory tests. A damaged item may need professional assessment.

guides.title: How to read laundry care symbols in order
guides.description: Start with the wash tub, then check bleach, drying, ironing and the professional-care circle. Each mark controls a different treatment, and an absent mark does
guides.lead: Start with the wash tub, then check bleach, drying, ironing and the professional-care circle. Each mark controls a different treatment, and an absent mark does not automatically authorize it.

sections.heading: 1. Read the sequence, not just one mark
body: International labels normally follow washing, bleaching, drying, ironing and professional care. The precise sequence helps prevent mixing a crossed dryer with a crossed wash tub.

sections.heading: 2. Read the modifiers
body: Numbers in a tub are maximum wash temperatures. One line under a symbol requests a milder process; two lines call for a very mild process. Dryer dots and iron dots have their own meanings.

sections.heading: 3. Check the finished article
body: The label accounts for the entire garment, including finishes, attached decoration and lining. Fibre composition alone cannot determine whether tumbling or bleaching is allowed.

sections.heading: 4. If a mark is missing or unreadable
body: Leave it unknown and consult the other written instructions or manufacturer. Our decoder does not infer permission from an empty slot.

guides.title: ISO vs ASTM care symbols: what actually differs?
guides.description: ISO 3758:2023 is the international standard. The U.S. has its own longstanding ASTM-based symbol convention; the public FTC-hosted chart reflects a historical
guides.lead: ISO 3758:2023 is the international standard. The U.S. has its own longstanding ASTM-based symbol convention; the public FTC-hosted chart reflects a historical edition, not the full 2025 ASTM standard.

sections.heading: Temperature inside the wash tub
body: International ISO tubs usually show a temperature number such as 30 or 40. The U.S. reference includes dot-based wash-temperature symbols. Never convert them by guesswork.

sections.heading: Ironing temperatures have changed
body: Current public ISO 2023 guides describe low, medium and high limits of 120°C, 160°C and 210°C. Older U.S. references commonly use 110°C, 150°C and 200°C. The decoder keeps these editions separate.

sections.heading: Current standard versus historical public chart
body: ASTM lists D5489-25 as active. Its licensed full content is not bundled here; we do not claim a historical FTC chart represents that entire new guide.

sections.heading: How to choose in the decoder
body: Use ISO for a number-in-tub international tag and the U.S. historical guide for a U.S. dot-based tag when it matches. When uncertain, compare against the original manufacturer’s instructions.

guides.description: A missing symbol is not proof that a treatment is allowed. When a label is partly faded or cut off, use written maker instructions, garment information and pro
guides.lead: A missing symbol is not proof that a treatment is allowed. When a label is partly faded or cut off, use written maker instructions, garment information and professional advice rather than reconstructing permissions from guesses.

sections.heading: Look for more than one label
body: Some garments have a side-seam care label and a separate composition label. Check removable components and manufacturer-provided care instructions.

sections.heading: Do not fill in invisible marks
body: If the dryer symbol is absent or too damaged to read, mark machine drying as unknown. The decoder intentionally leaves treatment categories incomplete.

sections.heading: Use photo magnification, not unsupported auto-recognition
body: A zoomed image may help you distinguish an underline, dot or diagonal stroke. Camera quality and folds can produce misleading shapes, so the final selection must be confirmed manually.

sections.heading: Ask for verified care details
body: For a valuable or unusual item, contact the manufacturer or a textile-care professional with a readable photo of the complete tag.

guides.title: I shrank a sweater: what can I do now?
guides.description: First identify whether the sweater felted or merely dried out of shape. Some distortion may respond to careful professional reshaping; felting is often not ful
guides.lead: First identify whether the sweater felted or merely dried out of shape. Some distortion may respond to careful professional reshaping; felting is often not fully reversible, so avoid promised “miracle fixes.”

sections.heading: Stop the damaging treatment
body: Do not run a second hot wash or tumble dry in an attempt to loosen fibres. Check the label and keep the sweater away from direct heat while deciding what to do.

sections.heading: Assess the change
body: A compact, dense surface suggests felting after heat and agitation. A garment stretched in one direction may have changed shape during wet hanging; that is a different problem.

sections.heading: Consider cautious reshaping only when permitted
body: If the garment may be wetted, gentle flat reshaping by hand may help some distortion. Do not use force or household chemicals based on viral tricks; consider a textile-care specialist for valuable items.

sections.heading: Prevent a repeat
body: Check the wash tub for very-mild and hand-wash marks, and the square for flat drying and no-tumble restrictions. Woolmark advises flat drying many wet wool sweaters.

guides.title: 30°C, 40°C, 60°C: what the wash numbers mean
guides.description: The number in an international washing tub is the maximum permissible water temperature for that garment and cycle. You may choose a cooler wash, but that does
guides.lead: The number in an international washing tub is the maximum permissible water temperature for that garment and cycle. You may choose a cooler wash, but that does not remove any gentle-cycle restriction.

sections.heading: 30°C and 40°C are not universal defaults
body: Many everyday garments use these limits, but colourfastness, trims and finishes still matter. A bar under the tub reduces agitation; it does not alter the numeric maximum.

sections.heading: 60°C and hotter need a specific label
body: Some household items allow higher temperatures, but never infer this from their cotton content. Read the tub and any printed text on the actual item.

sections.heading: Cooler is not always equally effective
body: A lower setting may clean less effectively for some soils or hygiene needs. Follow detergent and appliance directions and use an allowed temperature rather than exceeding the label.

sections.heading: U.S. dots are a separate reference
body: The historical U.S. chart includes numbered dot levels in the wash tub. Use the corresponding reference system rather than treating dots as an ISO temperature number.
